about_carthage_body: Punic stelae, Roman Africa proconsularis, and the Byrsa hill remain the oldest onomastic layer of Tunisian genealogy — names, places, and Mediterranean crossings that still echo in family memory.
about_civil_body: État civil from 1886 onward, Protectorate cadastre, and republican identity papers connect living families to the older documentary chain — 24 governorates, one indexed research surface.
about_cta_title: A Question About Your Tunisian Ancestors?
about_etat_civil_body: Birth, marriage, and death registers from 1886, indexed by governorate.
about_habous_body: Pious endowments tying families to olive groves, fondouks, and medina houses.
about_hero_p: In Tunisia, genealogical truth is never fabricated: it is firmly grounded in 19th and 20th-century registers. We bridge the gap between oral tradition and physical archive records without hype or artifice.
about_hero_subtitle: From Punic Carthage and Fatimid Kairouan to Ottoman sijillat and modern état civil, Roots Tunisia holds family evidence across twenty-four governorates.
about_kairouan_body: The Aghlabid and Fatimid capital preserved nasab chains, waqf deeds, and jurisprudential manuscripts. Kairouan remains a primary key for tracing scholarly and tribal lineages across the Sahel and the interior.
about_kairouan_panel_intro: Kairouan’s manuscript culture and pious endowments are not decoration. They are how families recorded descent, property, and scholarship from the Aghlabids through the Hafsids.
about_kairouan_panel_title: Nasab, waqf, and the Great Mosque
about_legal_desc: Roots Tunisia strictly complies with national and international laws governing public archives and personal privacy.
about_map_intro: Click a region to read its archival holdings and notable lineages — from Carthage and the Cap Bon to Djerba, the Djérid, and the northwest.
about_method_step_1_desc: We cross-examine ancestral nicknames, kunyas, and governorate origins against geographical registries and tribal confederation rolls.
about_method_step_2_desc: Court deeds, marriage contracts, and habous endowments establish unassailable legal parentage across centuries.
about_method_step_3_desc: Connecting 1886-present records with pre-colonial ancestry to render interactive D3 genealogical visualizations.
about_methodology_title: From oral lineage to verified documentary trees
about_mission_intro: Tunisian families are documented in more than one script, court, and language. A pedigree may begin with a CIN extract in Sousse, pass through a Tunis qadi sijill, and rest on a habous deed in Kairouan. Roots Tunisia keeps those layers together.
about_mission_title: Why Tunisian genealogy needs its own house
about_seo_desc: Roots Tunisia preserves Tunisian lineage through Carthage, Kairouan, Ottoman sijillat, civil registry, and the 24 governorates.
about_seo_title: About Roots Tunisia — Carthage to the civil registry
about_sijillat_body: Charaïque court registers, beylical decrees, and majba tax rolls document marriages, inheritances, and habous from Tunis, Sfax, and the medinas. These sijillat are the backbone of pre-colonial pedigree work.
about_sijillat_panel_intro: Sijillat from charaïque courts, beylical chancery, and majba rolls name spouses, witnesses, neighbourhoods, and estates. They sit beside Protectorate état civil rather than beneath it.
about_why_desc: What sets Roots Tunisia apart: uncompromising archival ethics, verifiable physical sources, and continuous presence in the field.

dossier_summary_all_tunisia: Tunisia's genealogical heritage spans 24 governorates uniting Mediterranean coastal ports, Andalusian-settled valleys, Roman-Berber high plains, and Saharan oases.
dossier_summary_central_west: Anchored by Kairouan — fourth holiest city of Islam and capital of medieval Ifriqiya — alongside the Byzantine-Roman high steppes of Sbeitla (Kasserine) and Sidi Bouzid.
dossier_summary_greater_tunis: Encompassing Tunis, Ariana, Ben Arous, and Manouba, Greater Tunis has served as the political, scholarly, and commercial heart of Tunisia since the Hafsid Sultanate.
dossier_summary_north: Strategic Mediterranean port region anchored by Bizerte, ancient Utica, and the Andalusian-Ottoman naval harbor of Ghar El Melh (Porto Farina).
dossier_summary_north_east: Fertile peninsula of Nabeul, Hammamet, Kelibia, and Soliman paired with the mountain springs of Zaghouan — Tunisia's premier heartland of Andalusian Morisco heritage.
dossier_summary_north_west: Uniting Béja, Jendouba, El Kef, and Siliana across the fertile Medjerda valley, Khroumirie forests, and historic fortress cities of the Tell.
dossier_summary_sahel: Historic coastal belt of olive groves, Aghlabid ribats, Fatimid capitals, and ancient merchant towns stretching from Sousse and Monastir to Mahdia and El Jem.
dossier_summary_south_east: From the walled merchant medina of Sfax and the coastal oasis of Gabès to the island of Djerba and the fortified Amazigh hilltop ksour of Medenine and Tataouine.
dossier_summary_south_west: Spanning Gafsa, Tozeur, and Kebili around Chott el-Djerid — a storied region of prehistoric Capsian sites, palm oases, scholar-poets, and trans-Saharan caravan routes.

gov_desc_ariana: Northern metropolitan plain known for its historic Andalusian gardens, rose cultivation, and Beylical summer palaces.
gov_desc_beja: Ancient Numidian Vaga, granary of Rome, nestled in the fertile Medjerda valley alongside Dougga and the Andalusian town of Testour.
gov_desc_ben_arous: Southern gateway to Tunis along the Gulf, home to Radès, Hammam-Lif thermal springs, Mornag vineyards, and Mount Boukornine.
gov_desc_bizerte: Northernmost point of Africa (Cap Angela), historic port city, ancient Utica, and Andalusian-Ottoman harbor of Ghar El Melh.
gov_desc_gabes: Ancient Tacapae: the Mediterranean's unique coastal palm oasis (Chenini, Jara, Menzel) paired with the Amazigh troglodyte hills of Matmata.
gov_desc_gafsa: Ancient Capsa — cradle of the prehistoric Capsian civilization — renowned for its Roman thermal pools, historic oasis, and mining basin.
gov_desc_jendouba: Home to the subterranean Roman villas of Bulla Regia, ancient Numidian Chemtou, Tabarka coral coast, and Ain Draham oak forests.
gov_desc_kairouan: Spiritual and scholarly capital of the Maghreb founded in 670 CE by Uqba ibn Nafi; seat of the Aghlabid dynasty and Maliki jurists.
gov_desc_kasserine: High steppe crossroads beneath Mount Chaambi (Tunisia's highest peak), encompassing Roman-Byzantine Sufetula (Sbeitla) and Cillium.
gov_desc_kebili: Heart of the Nefzaoua oases between Chott el-Djerid and the Grand Erg Oriental dunes, anchored by Kebili and Douz, Gateway to the Sahara.
gov_desc_le_kef: Highland citadel city (Sicca Veneria) near Table de Jugurtha, historic cultural crossroads of Sufi orders, music, and scholarship.
gov_desc_mahdia: 10th-century Fatimid Caliphate capital on a fortified peninsula, renowned for silk weaving, Skifa Kahla, and the El Jem Amphitheatre.
gov_desc_manouba: Fertile lower Medjerda plains, sanctuary of Lella Manoubia, Andalusian town of Tebourba, and historic Beylical Rose Palace.
gov_desc_medenine: Uniting the UNESCO World Heritage Island of Djerba, the coastal peninsula of Zarzis, and the vaulted ghorfa ksour of Medenine and Beni Khedache.
gov_desc_monastir: Ancient Ruspina, 796 CE coastal Ribat fortress of Harthama ibn A'yan, textile guilds of Ksar Hellal, and birthplace of Habib Bourguiba.
gov_desc_nabeul: The Cap Bon peninsula: ceramic guilds of Nabeul, Andalusian town of Soliman, citrus groves of Beni Khalled, and Kelibia fortress.
gov_desc_sfax: Southern economic capital with an intact 9th-century walled Medina, suburban borj garden estates (jnens), and the Kerkennah Islands.
gov_desc_sidi_bouzid: Central agricultural steppes and pastoral plains around Mount Bouhedma, historic homeland of the Hammama confederation.
gov_desc_siliana: Highlands of the Tunisian Dorsal housing the Numidian-Roman city of Mactaris (Makthar) and the ancient site of Zama Regia.
gov_desc_sousse: The Pearl of the Sahel: Punic-Roman Hadrumetum, 9th-century Aghlabid Ribat and Great Mosque, and thriving coastal merchant city.
gov_desc_tataouine: Southern Dahar plateau famed for its multi-story fortified granaries (Ksar Ouled Soltane, Ksar Ezzahra) and hilltop Amazigh villages of Chenini and Douiret.
gov_desc_tozeur: Capital of Bled el-Djerid, famed for Ouled el-Hadef brick architecture, Ibn Chabbat's hydraulic canals, Nefta's Sufi zawiyas, and Abu al-Qasim al-Shabbi.
gov_desc_tunis: Capital of the Republic, historic seat of the Husainid Beys, ancient Carthage, and spiritual center of Zitouna University.
gov_desc_zaghouan: Mountain spring supplying ancient Carthage with water via the Roman Aqueduct, and historic Morisco haven famous for rosewater.

guide_step1_desc: Present your National Identity Card (CIN) or Passport at the reception desk. A personal researcher card is issued on-site granting reading room access.
guide_step2_desc: Consult the paper inventories or online OPAC to find the archival classification (Série, Carton, Registre). Submit up to 3 call slips per research session.
guide_step3_desc: General administrative records become public after 30 years. Civil registry and judicial inheritance records protect personal privacy for 100 years unless direct ascendance is legally proven.
guide_step4_desc: Non-flash personal photography is permitted for most public series. High-resolution certified reproductions can be ordered at the digital laboratory desk.
help_a_create_account: Click Sign Up in the top navigation, enter your name, email, and password. You will receive immediate access to start building your trees.
help_a_data_rights: You have full rights under data protection laws to access, correct, export in GEDCOM, or permanently erase your data via your profile.
help_a_delete_account: Go to User Settings in your dashboard, find Danger Zone, and submit an account erasure request. Your personal trees and profile will be permanently deleted.
help_a_first_tree: From your dashboard, choose 'New Tree', set privacy preferences, and add ancestors or import an existing GEDCOM file in one click.
help_a_forgot_password: Click 'Forgot Password' on the login screen, enter your email address, and follow the instructions sent to reset your credentials securely.
help_a_gedcom_import: We support GEDCOM 5.5.1, GEDCOM 7.0, and GEDCOM X (XML, JSON, or .gedx). Use the Import GEDCOM button inside the builder toolbar.
help_a_how_to_pay: Choose a plan, submit payment via bank transfer or local methods (D17/Flouci in Tunisia or cards), and upload a screenshot of your receipt as proof.
help_a_language: Yes — Roots Tunisia fully supports 6 languages: Arabic, French, English, Spanish, Italian, and Maltese via the top navigation switcher.
help_a_payment_review_time: Most submissions are reviewed within 2 to 24 hours. You receive an instant notification once your tier is activated.
help_a_plans_differ: Basic is free for exploration. Premium unlocks full digitized archives and trees. Historian Pro provides direct paleography support and priority assistance.
help_a_request_download: Open the tree and click 'Request Download'. The owner receives a notification and can approve or decline via their dashboard.
help_a_view_vs_download: Viewing public trees is open, but downloading raw GEDCOM files requires owner approval to protect family researchers from unauthorized duplication.
help_a_who_sees_tree: You control privacy: private trees are visible only to you; public trees appear in the gallery with living person protections.

period_aghabid_note: Scholarly chains of transmission among Kairouan jurists provide Tunisia’s oldest continuous recorded lineages.
period_aghabid_records: Kairouan biographical dictionaries (tabaqat), nasab lineage chains, early waqf deeds.
period_contemporary_note: Collaborative digital genealogy reconnects diaspora branches across the Mediterranean and beyond.
period_contemporary_records: Digitized civil databases, municipal registries, oral history testimonies, and archival restorations.
period_context_body: Contextualize your ancestors across Aghlabid, Hafsid, Andalusian, Ottoman Beylical, Protectorate, and modern eras.
period_hafsid_note: Tunis emerges as imperial capital; mercantile, scholarly, and Andalusian refugee families appear in continuous records.
period_hafsid_records: Hafsid chancery registers, qadi court rulings, family endowment deeds (habous), and scholar ijazat.
period_independence_note: The Code of Personal Status unifies family law, creating modern verifiable civil lineages across Tunisia.
period_independence_records: National civil registry, CIN identity cards, nationality files, and municipal rolls.
period_ottoman_note: The richest pre-modern documentary layer: inheritance and marriage cases systematically name three to four generations.
period_ottoman_records: Charaïque court sijillat, habous deeds, beylical decrees, majba tax registers, and corporation rolls.
period_protectorate_note: Systematic civil registration begins in 1886; fixed family surnames become formalized across all governorates.
period_protectorate_records: État civil registers, cadastre land titles, caïdat files, Sadiki and school registers, ANOM records.
period_punic_note: No unbroken lineage records survive, but ancestral names and territorial toponyms persist in Tunisian heritage.
period_punic_records: Votive stelae from the Tophet, Punic onomastics, Neo-Punic commemorative inscriptions.
period_roman_note: Latin inscriptions document family groupings, civic magistrates, and freedmen across Tunisian cities.
period_roman_records: Funerary epigraphy, municipal alba, land surveys, El Jem and Dougga inscriptions.
period_vandal_note: Ecclesiastical records predominate; onomastic transitions reflect demographic evolution in urban centres.
period_vandal_records: Ecclesiastical councils, episcopal lists, Christian Latin funerary texts, and fortress foundations.

about_mission_p1: Too often, the search for ancestral origins in North Africa faces approximations or sourceless claims. At Roots Tunisia, our standard is uncompromising: verifiable genealogy begins with primary documentary evidence.
about_mission_p2: We identify, cross-reference and examine authentic archival holdings documenting Muslim, Jewish, Italian and Maltese communities across Tunisia.

about_why_3_desc: Each record, individual or lineage links to a verifiable physical shelfmark (register, box, folio). We reject presumed genealogies lacking archival foundation.

gov_desc_alexandria_port: Northernmost point of Africa (Cap Angela), historic port city, ancient Utica, and Andalusian-Ottoman harbor of Ghar El Melh.
gov_desc_aswan: Southern Dahar plateau famed for its multi-story fortified granaries (Ksar Ouled Soltane, Ksar Ezzahra) and hilltop Amazigh villages of Chenini and Douiret.
gov_desc_asyut: Ancient Capsa — cradle of the prehistoric Capsian civilization — renowned for its Roman thermal pools, historic oasis, and mining basin.
gov_desc_beheira: Ancient Numidian Vaga, granary of Rome, nestled in the fertile Nile Valley valley alongside Dougga and the Andalusian town of Testour.
gov_desc_beni_suef: High steppe crossroads beneath Mount Chaambi (Tunisia's highest peak), encompassing Roman-Byzantine Sufetula (Sbeitla) and Cillium.
gov_desc_cairo_azhar: Spiritual, political and scholarly capital of Tunisia founded in 969 CE by the Fatimids; seat of Al-Azhar and Citadel archives.
gov_desc_damietta: The Nile Delta peninsula: ceramic guilds of Damiette, Andalusian town of Soliman, citrus groves of Beni Khalled, and Kelibia fortress.
gov_desc_faiyum: Mountain spring supplying ancient Thebes / Memphis with water via the Roman Aqueduct, and historic Morisco haven famous for rosewater.
gov_desc_giza: The Cradle of Monuments: Giza Pyramids, Saqqara, ancient Memphis, and fertile agricultural estates of the western Nile.
gov_desc_ismailia: Home to the subterranean Roman villas of Bulla Regia, ancient Numidian Chemtou, Tabarka coral coast, and Ain Draham oak forests.
gov_desc_luxor: Capital of Bled el-Djerid, famed for Ouled el-Hadef brick architecture, Ibn Chabbat's hydraulic canals, Nefta's Sufi zawiyas, and Abu al-Qasim al-Shabbi.
gov_desc_mansoura: Southern economic capital with an intact 9th-century walled Medina, suburban borj garden estates (jnens), and the Kerkennah Islands.
gov_desc_new_valley: Heart of the Nefzaoua oases between Chott el-Djerid and the Grand Erg Oriental dunes, anchored by Nouvelle-Vallée and Douz, Gateway to the Sahara.
gov_desc_qalyubia: Highlands of the Tunisiaian Dorsal housing the Numidian-Roman city of Mactaris (Makthar) and the ancient site of Zama Regia.
gov_desc_sinai: Sinai Peninsula connecting the Gulf of Suez, Mount Sinai, Saint Catherine monastery, and Red Sea trading routes.
gov_desc_suez: Ancient Tacapae: the Mediterranean's unique coastal palm oasis (Chenini, Jara, Menzel) paired with the Amazigh troglodyte hills of Matmata.
gov_desc_tanta: Delta capital in Gharbia renowned for the Sayyid al-Badawi mosque, textile traditions, and agricultural trade.
gov_desc_zagazig: Ancient Ruspina, 796 CE coastal Ribat fortress of Harthama ibn A'yan, textile guilds of Ksar Hellal, and birthplace of Habib Bourguiba.

legacy.about_carthage_body: Punic stelae, Roman Africa proconsularis, and the Byrsa hill remain the oldest onomastic layer of Tunisiaian genealogy — names, places, and Mediterranean crossings that still echo in family memory.
legacy.about_civil_body: État civil from 1886 onward, Protectorate cadastre, and republican identity papers connect living families to the older documentary chain — 24 governorates, one indexed research surface.

legacy.about_etat_civil_body: Birth, marriage, and death registers from 1886, indexed by governorate.
legacy.about_habous_body: Pious endowments tying families to olive groves, fondouks, and medina houses.
legacy.about_hero_p: in Tunisia, genealogical truth is never fabricated: it is firmly grounded in 19th and 20th-century registers. We bridge the gap between oral tradition and physical archive records without hype or artifice.
legacy.about_hero_subtitle: From Pharaonic Thebes and Fatimid Tunis to Ottoman sijillat and modern état civil, Roots Tunisia holds family evidence across twenty-four governorates.
legacy.about_hero_title: A Tunisiaian archive of names, places, and periods
legacy.about_legal_desc: Roots Tunisia strictly complies with national and international laws governing public archives and personal privacy.
legacy.about_map_intro: Click a region to read its archival holdings and notable lineages — from Thebes / Memphis and the Nile Delta to Alexandrie, the Djérid, and the northwest.
legacy.about_method_step_1_desc: We cross-examine ancestral nicknames, kunyas, and governorate origins against geographical registries and tribal confederation rolls.
legacy.about_method_step_2_desc: Court deeds, marriage contracts, and waqf endowments establish unassailable legal parentage across centuries.
legacy.about_method_step_3_desc: Connecting 1886-present records with pre-colonial ancestry to render interactive D3 genealogical visualizations.
legacy.about_methodology_title: From oral lineage to verified documentary trees
legacy.about_mission_intro: Tunisiaian families are documented in more than one script, court, and language. A pedigree may begin with a modern civil extract, pass through a Tunis qadi sijill, and rest on a waqf deed in Kasbah Archives. Roots Tunisia keeps those layers together.
legacy.about_mission_title: Why Tunisiaian genealogy needs its own house
legacy.about_seo_desc: Roots Tunisia preserves Tunisiaian lineage through Thebes / Memphis, Al-Azhar / Tunis, Ottoman sijillat, civil registry, and the 24 governorates.
legacy.about_seo_title: About Roots Tunisia — Thebes / Memphis to the civil registry
legacy.about_sijillat_body: Charaïque court registers, khedival decrees, and ta'dad tax rolls document marriages, inheritances, and waqf deeds in Tunis, Mansoura, and across the 24 governorates. These sijillats are the bedrock of Tunisiaian genealogical inquiry.
legacy.about_sijillat_panel_intro: Sijillat from charaïque courts, khedival chancery, and ta'dad rolls name spouses, witnesses, neighbourhoods, and estates. They sit beside Protectorate état civil rather than beneath it.
legacy.about_why_desc: What sets Roots Tunisia apart: uncompromising archival ethics, verifiable physical sources, and continuous presence in the field.

legacy.guide_step1_desc: Present your National Identity Card (CIN) or Passport at the reception desk. A personal researcher card is issued on-site granting reading room access.
legacy.guide_step2_desc: Consult the paper inventories or online OPAC to find the archival classification (Série, Carton, Registre). Submit up to 3 call slips per research session.
legacy.guide_step3_desc: General administrative records become public after 30 years. Civil registry and judicial inheritance records protect personal privacy for 100 years unless direct ascendance is legally proven.
legacy.guide_step4_desc: Non-flash personal photography is permitted for most public series. High-resolution certified reproductions can be ordered at the digital laboratory desk.

legacy.period_hafsid_note: Tunis emerges as imperial capital; mercantile, scholarly, and Andalusian refugee families appear in continuous records.
legacy.period_hafsid_records: Hafsid chancery registers, qadi court rulings, family endowment deeds (habous), and scholar ijazat.
legacy.period_independence_note: The Code of Personal Status unifies family law, creating modern verifiable civil lineages across Tunisia.
legacy.period_independence_records: National civil registry, CIN identity cards, nationality files, and municipal rolls.
legacy.period_ottoman_note: The richest pre-modern documentary layer: inheritance and marriage cases systematically name three to four generations.
legacy.period_ottoman_records: Sharia court sijillats (Mahkamat al-Bab al-Ali), waqf deeds, Khedival decrees, and Ta'dad an-Nufus population censuses.
legacy.period_protectorate_note: Systematic civil registration begins in 1886; fixed family surnames become formalized across all governorates.
legacy.period_protectorate_records: État civil registers, cadastre land titles, caïdat files, Sadiki and school registers, ANOM records.
legacy.period_punic_note: No unbroken lineage records survive, but ancestral names and territorial toponyms persist in Tunisiaian heritage.
legacy.period_punic_records: Pharaonic temple inscriptions, demotic papyri, Ptolemaic censuses, and Greco-Roman burial inscriptions.
legacy.period_roman_note: Latin inscriptions document family groupings, civic magistrates, and freedmen across Tunisiaian cities.
legacy.period_roman_records: Papyri fragments, temple inscriptions, land surveys (Kharaj), and Greco-Roman registries.
legacy.period_vandal_note: Ecclesiastical records predominate; onomastic transitions reflect demographic evolution in urban centres.
legacy.period_vandal_records: Ecclesiastical councils, episcopal lists, Christian Latin funerary texts, and fortress foundations.
